title: Find All Anagrams in a String
description: Brute force to optimized: recounting every window versus an incrementally maintained sliding window count.

sections.title: Find All Anagrams in a String

content.title: Find All Anagrams in a String

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given two strings s and p, return every starting index in s where a substring of the same length as p is an anagram of p.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Problem Summary","Return every starting index in s where a length-of-p substring is an anagram of p."],["Input","s, a string of length n, and p, a string of length m, m typically much smaller than n."],["Output","A list of integers, every valid starting index, in any order."],["Constraints","1 <= s.length, p.length <= 30000, both strings consist of lowercase English letters."],["Requirements","Every window checked must be exactly the same length as p, and its letters must match p's letters exactly, in any order."]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Pattern","A fixed size sliding window with an incrementally maintained letter count, compared against p's fixed count."],["Difficulty","Intermediate"],["Tags","Strings, Sliding Window, Hash Table"],["Interview Focus","Recognizing that a window's letter count can be updated by adding one character and removing one character, instead of being rebuilt from scratch at every position."]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given two strings s and p, return every starting index in s where a substring of the same length as p is an anagram of p.

blocks.title: Analogy: Spotting Every Rearranged Match in a Longer Text
blocks.text: Like sliding a fixed size window across a long strip of text, checking at every position whether the letters currently inside the window are exactly a rearrangement of a target word.

blocks.caption: Every window whose letters exactly match the pattern's letters counts as a match

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: s = "cbaebabacd", p = "abc"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Window \"cba\" (indices 0 to 2) uses the same letters as \"abc\"","a match at index 0","both use exactly one a, one b, and one c"],["Window \"bac\" (indices 6 to 8) also uses the same letters","a match at index 6","both use exactly one a, one b, and one c"],["Answer","[0, 6]","these are the only two windows whose letters exactly match p"]]}

blocks.text: Example: s = "abab", p = "ab"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Every window of length 2 starting at indices 0, 1, 2 uses only a and b","all three positions match","each window contains exactly one a and one b, regardless of their order"],["Answer","[0, 1, 2]","every possible window of this length is a valid anagram of p"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: p longer than s
If p is longer than s, no window of that size can even fit inside s, so the answer is an empty list.
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask how much actually changes between one window and the very next one right beside it.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Valid Anagram already showed exactly how to detect whether two strings are anagrams, by comparing their letter counts, and that comparison, against p's fixed count, is exactly what every window here needs to pass.

Observation 2: The brute force rebuilds a window's letter count completely from scratch at every position, even though consecutive windows overlap in all but two characters.

Observation 3: Sliding Window Maximum already showed that a window's summary can be updated incrementally as it slides forward, adding the newly included element and removing the one that just fell out, instead of recomputing it from nothing.

Observation 4: Applying that same incremental update directly to letter counts here, adding the new character entering the window and subtracting the one leaving it, turns every window transition into constant time work, confirmed by tracing s equal to "cbaebabacd" against p equal to "abc" through to the correct matches at indices 0 and 6.

Recognizing that a sliding window's letter count only ever changes by one character entering and one character leaving is what replaces rebuilding every window from scratch with a single incremental update per step.
6. Brute Force Solution
For every possible window of length equal to p, count the letters inside that window from scratch and compare those counts directly against p's own letter counts.
Step by step algorithm

items: Precompute the letter counts of p once.
For every window of the same length in s, count that window's letters completely from scratch.
If the window's counts match p's counts exactly, record its starting index.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: p's letter counts are computed exactly once, up front, since they never change across the whole search.
Each window's count map is rebuilt completely fresh, so no information from the previous window position is ever reused.
A direct equality check between the two count maps confirms whether the window is a true anagram of p.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every window's letter counts are directly compared against p's counts, so every true anagram match is correctly found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times m), recounting up to m letters for each of roughly n window positions.
Space: O(m), for the count maps.
Limitation: consecutive windows overlap in all but two positions, yet each window's letter counts are rebuilt completely from scratch instead of being adjusted incrementally.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: rebuilding an entire window's letter count from scratch throws away almost all of the previous window's already correct counts, since only two characters actually change between consecutive windows.

What an incrementally maintained count fixes directly: adding the one new character entering the window and subtracting the one character leaving it keeps the running count correct with constant work per step.

What has to be tracked carefully: the character leaving the window is always the one m positions behind the current one, so that subtraction must only happen once the window has fully formed.

The core idea: slide the window one character at a time, updating counts incrementally, and compare against p's fixed count at every valid window position.

Slide a window of fixed size across s, maintaining a running letter count for the current window instead of rebuilding it. When the window moves forward by one, add the newly included character's count and subtract the count of the character that just fell out of the window on the left. Compare this running count against p's fixed count at every position.
9. Optimized Solution
A sliding window with an incrementally maintained letter count.
Dry run for s = "cbaebabacd", p = "abc" (window size 3)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Window start","Window contents","Action"],"rows":[["0","\"cba\"","counts match p exactly, record index 0"],["1","\"bae\"","add e, remove c: counts no longer match"],["2","\"aeb\"","add b, remove b: counts still do not match"],["6","\"bac\"","counts match p exactly, record index 6"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: maintain the window's letter counts incrementally as it slides

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because incrementally adding the newly entering character and removing the one that just left keeps the running count exactly equal to the true letter count of the current window at every single step, so comparing that running count against p's fixed count at each position correctly identifies every true anagram match.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["The window has not yet reached its full size of m characters","Only characters are added, none are removed yet","The count correctly builds up toward the first full window"],["The window has reached its full size and slides forward by one","One character is added and exactly one is removed","The running count always reflects exactly the current window's contents"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with constant work per character.
Space: O(1), two fixed size 26 element count arrays.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Reuses Prior Work","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Brute force (recount every window)","O(n times m)","O(m)","No, every window rebuilt from scratch","Correct, but wasteful whenever s is much longer than p."],["Optimized (incremental sliding window)","O(n)","O(1)","Yes, only one character changes per step","The expected answer, the standard fixed size sliding window pattern."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
This is the standard fixed size sliding window pattern with incremental counts, the same idea used across many "find all windows matching some frequency condition" problems.
Common Mistakes

items: Comparing the full 26 element count arrays on every single step, which is correct but adds a constant factor of 26 comparisons per position, when an incrementally tracked "number of matching letters" counter can make each step truly constant time.
Forgetting to remove the character that falls out of the window on the left once the window has slid past its very first position.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["p longer than s","No window can even fit and the answer is empty."],["p and s being identical","Matches at exactly one position, index 0."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Mention the further micro optimization of tracking a single integer counter for "how many of the 26 letters currently have matching counts" instead of comparing two full arrays every step, which turns the comparison itself into O(1) instead of O(26).

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid recounting every window", think: an incrementally maintained sliding window count, adding and removing one character per step.
If the interviewer says "can you make the comparison itself O(1) too", think: track a single "matching letters" counter instead of comparing two full 26 element arrays.
If the interviewer says "what if the alphabet were larger than 26 letters", think: swap the fixed size arrays for hash maps, the sliding window logic stays identical.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why is it safe to compare the running window count against p's count only once the window has reached its full size?
How would you make the per step comparison itself O(1) instead of O(26)?
How would you adapt this approach to find windows that are anagrams of any one of several different target strings?
How would this approach change if the alphabet were not limited to 26 lowercase letters?
How would you count the total number of matching windows without materializing every starting index?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Valid Anagram, whose letter count comparison is the exact check performed at every window position here.
Sliding Window Maximum, whose incrementally maintained window summary is the same instinct applied here to letter counts instead of a running maximum.
Group Anagrams, which uses a related canonical letter signature idea, but for grouping many separate strings rather than scanning windows of one longer string.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n times m) time, O(m) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(1) space (fixed 26 letter count arrays).
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a fixed size sliding window with an incrementally maintained letter count, compared against p's fixed count.

Core Idea: only one character enters and one character leaves the window at each step, so its letter count can be updated incrementally rather than rebuilt from scratch, turning each window check into constant time work.
Time: O(n times m) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(m) for the brute force, O(1) for the optimized approach's fixed size count arrays.
Most Important Observation: consecutive windows differ by exactly one character on each side, which is precisely what makes an incremental update possible.
Interview Difficulty: the sliding window idea is standard; proactively mentioning the O(1) match-counter micro optimization is what shows extra polish.
One line memory trick: add the entering character, remove the leaving one, compare against p's fixed count.
